content.text:
Good — the listings tell us a lot about what each will *test* in interviews. Here's the comparison through that lens.

The most striking pattern: Anthropic's PM listings repeatedly bake in an *explicit engineering requirement*. Claude Code asks for "5+ years... including at least 1 year as a professional engineer." Others say "engineering background and 2+ years in PM." For you, transitioning from SWE, that's a tailwind — Anthropic literally screens for the thing you already have, and the interview will probe your technical depth as a feature, not a nice-to-have. Expect them to test whether you can reason about model behavior, evals, and agent architecture concretely.

OpenAI's listings read differently. They're organized around *deployment surfaces and stakeholder complexity* — Integrity, Countries & Governments, Families. The recurring phrase is collaboration "with product, safety, policy, user operations and engineering." So OpenAI interviews lean harder on product sense in messy, high-stakes, multi-stakeholder situations: safety tradeoffs, policy constraints, "this product touches millions and could harm people" judgment. Less "prove you can code," more "prove you can navigate ambiguity and tradeoffs responsibly."

So if I compress what each *tests*:

- Anthropic: technical credibility is a gate. Be ready to go deep on how agents/evals/models actually work. Your SWE background is your edge here.
- OpenAI: product judgment under safety/policy pressure, stakeholder orchestration, and AI hands-on experience all together — that aakashgupta piece called it product sense + technical depth + hands-on AI, all three.

Both share the safety framing, but Anthropic puts it inside the technical work while OpenAI puts it inside the product/policy work.

One caveat: these are snapshots of a handful of req's, and listings vary a lot by team. The interview *loop* itself — the actual rounds and what each round scores — isn't usually in the job post.

That last point might be worth its own space. Want me to spin up a child node on the interview loop structure (rounds, formats, what each scores)? It's a meatier topic than the requirements comparison.
